info.title: g1t API
info.description: The REST API for g1t, a git forge built for agents. The same operations are available to agents as MCP tools at https://mcp.g1t.sh. Every name in a request or response body is `snake_case`; names you chose, such as a workflow's inputs or a secret's name, are returned as you wrote them.

tags.name: Accounts
tags.description: Signing in from a tool, who a token acts as, and your email addresses.

tags.name: Notifications
tags.description: Your inbox: a thread for each thing you were told about (a work item, a pull request, a workflow on a branch, a deployment), why you were told, and what you subscribe to and watch. Your own: personal tokens and sessions only.

tags.name: Pinned projects
tags.description: The projects you keep at the top of a workspace's sidebar, in your order, up to eight a workspace. Your own: personal tokens and sessions only.

tags.name: Projects
tags.description: A project is what a workspace builds and runs, from a repository or a root directory in one. Each says what it is, where it runs and where to find it: its homepage, docs and other links.

tags.name: Workspaces
tags.description: A workspace owns repositories and is the first part of their address. People and agents work in workspaces.

tags.name: Getting started
tags.description: Each person's own state of a workspace's setup guide, which opens on its Home for its owners until they finish or dismiss it: whether they dismissed it, and the steps they skipped. Whether a step is done is read from the workspace itself. People only, each their own.

tags.name: Personal access tokens
tags.description: A workspace's rules for its members' personal access tokens: whether tokens made for all of a member's workspaces reach it, whether tokens may be made for it alone and wait for an owner's approval, and how long a token may last; the tokens that reach it, approving or denying the ones that wait, and revoking one there. Owners only, as people.

tags.name: Single sign-on
tags.description: A workspace's own identity provider over OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0 or SAML 2.0, on every paid plan: setting it up, requiring it of members, the people linked to it, unlinking one, and SCIM, through which the provider assigns and unassigns people at /scim/v2/{workspace}. People sign in to g1t as themselves and then through the provider to use the workspace; owners are never held out. Owners only, as people.

tags.name: Members
tags.description: A workspace's members and owners: who belongs to it, their roles (owner or member, with billing manager and security manager on top), handing it to another member, and leaving it.

tags.name: Invites
tags.description: Inviting a friend to g1t by email, inviting people into a workspace by username or email, and answering the invitations to workspaces sent to you. Anyone can sign up for g1t without an invite.

tags.name: Billing
tags.description: A workspace's usage, its budget and its invoices. Members read them; owners change the budget, as people. A run's token never changes billing.

tags.name: Repositories
tags.description: A repository, how it handles pull requests, and its timeline: renaming, archiving, moving and deleting it; and its files at a branch, tag or commit as a tarball or zipball.

tags.name: Commit comments
tags.description: Comments on a commit, as a whole or on one line of a file it changed. Anyone who can read a repository reads them, and may comment unless the repository turned commit comments off.

tags.name: Repository insights
tags.description: What a repository's default branch says about it, read in the background and kept by commit: the languages it is written in, who made it, and its license.

tags.name: Stars
tags.description: Starring a repository, to keep it and to say you like it: who starred one, and what you starred.

tags.name: Releases
tags.description: A release is a tag published with a title and notes. The latest is the newest published one that is neither a draft nor a prerelease.

tags.name: Access
tags.description: Who can do what in a repository: repository roles, people given a role on one repository (outside collaborators when they are not members), invitations, a workspace's base permission, and deploy keys: SSH keys that reach one repository.

tags.name: Teams
tags.description: Groups of a workspace's members: given a role on repositories together, mentioned together as @workspace/team, and asked to review together. Any member may create a team; the workspace's owners and the team's maintainers manage it.

tags.name: Security
tags.description: Secrets found in what is pushed and in a repository's history, and dependencies with known vulnerabilities: listing the alerts, and dismissing or reopening them.

tags.name: Secret scanning
tags.description: Secrets found in pushes and history, where each one is, pushing past push protection with a reason (and asking for approval when the workspace delegates bypasses), checking with a secret's issuer whether it still works, and custom patterns.

tags.name: Code scanning
tags.description: Results of static analysis tools, uploaded as SARIF: alerts on the default branch, the analyses that made them, uploads, and putting g1t on an alert to fix it.

tags.name: Supply chain
tags.description: What a repository depends on: vulnerability alerts, the dependency graph, an SPDX SBOM of it, and comparing two commits' dependencies as dependency review does.

tags.name: Security settings
tags.description: When pull request checks fail, dependency review's policy, delegated bypass and validity checks, and a workspace's security overview.

tags.name: Security advisories
tags.description: What a repository says about vulnerabilities in what it ships: advisories drafted, published and withdrawn by its maintainers, and the vulnerability reports people send them privately when the repository takes them.

tags.name: Rules
tags.description: Rulesets: what may happen to a repository's branches and tags and what a pull request needs before it merges, for a repository or across a workspace; the rules that hold for one branch; and how they judged each push and merge, with insights.

tags.name: Checks
tags.description: What CI, integrations and g1t Actions say about a commit, in the shapes CI tools already send: statuses (a state per context) and check runs (a lifecycle, a conclusion, a Markdown report, annotations on lines and buttons), grouped per reporter into check suites. g1t Actions jobs are check runs too. Required checks are met by either.

tags.name: Work items
tags.description: A workspace's tracked work (features, bugs, chores), numbered in the workspace's sequence with its new pull requests, and linked to the repositories it concerns: its origin (where it was filed), its targets (where the work is meant to land) and those it touched. A work item closes once what closes it has landed in every target. With comments, reactions, labels and decisions; and what `#N` names where it is written.

tags.name: Labels and milestones
tags.description: A workspace's labels, which its work items and pull requests carry by name, and its milestones, which gather them under a goal and a due date.

tags.name: Work projects
tags.description: A workspace's projects: homes for bodies of work, each with a brief, a lead and its people, the repositories its work lands in, dates, a state and a health. A work item is in one project or none.

tags.name: Pull requests
tags.description: A proposed change in its own fork or on a branch, with its comments and reactions. Several can be made for one work item, in its repositories; each merged one lands it in its repository. It merges by a merge commit, a squash, a rebase or a fast-forward, now or with auto-merge once everything it needs is met.

tags.name: Sessions
tags.description: Who is working on what, and how a pull request was made. A session is one run of your own harness (a Claude Code session, a Codex run) on a repository: started once, kept alive by heartbeats, attached to a work item and a pull request, and recording prompts, reasoning, the tools that ran, the skills used and what it touched. Each subagent is a session of its own under the one that started it. A pull request's session shows what was recorded on it. A session can also be started on a work item in your own Claude, on the workspace's Anthropic account.

tags.name: Decisions and why
tags.description: Decision records: why the work is the way it is, and how sure that is (claimed, tested by a check or the merge queue, or approved by a person). And why a line of code is the way it is: its commit, pull request, work item, decisions and session.

tags.name: Search
tags.description: One search across all of g1t: repositories, code, work items, pull requests, people and workspaces. Public content for everyone, and private content in workspaces you belong to.

tags.name: Actions
tags.description: GitHub Actions workflows in .g1t/workflows, their runs, their jobs' logs, their artifacts, and the repository's actions/cache entries.

tags.name: Packages
tags.description: A workspace's packages in every registry: their versions and download counts, deleting and restoring them within 30 days, their visibility and repository, the people and teams with a role on them, and which repositories' workflows may use them (Manage Actions access). A package is named by its type and its name, URL-encoded where it holds a slash.

tags.name: Deployments
tags.description: A repository's deployments wherever they run: reported from any CI with these routes, made by g1t Actions jobs with an `environment:`, or built on g1t.page. Each has statuses, shows on its commit as the check `deploy / <environment>`, and belongs to an environment.

tags.name: Observability
tags.description: What a project's running software did: its requests, logs, traces, grouped errors and metrics, from its apps on g1t.page with nothing to set up and from OpenTelemetry (OTLP over HTTP) sent from anywhere with an ingest token. Reading needs a role of your own on the project's repository; resolving errors, Triage; settings, ingest tokens, exports and usage, Admin.

tags.name: Run protection
tags.description: What keeps workflow runs safe: environments' protection rules (required reviewers, a wait timer, which branches may deploy) and the reviews of the jobs they hold, approving a pull request's run from outside, what a job's token gets when its workflow writes no `permissions:`, and repository_dispatch, which a job's own token may send.

tags.name: Secrets and variables
tags.description: Values that workflows and deployments read, per repository or for a whole workspace, with a row per environment.

tags.name: Runners
tags.description: Self-hosted runners: your own machines, which run your workflow jobs for $0 of g1t compute. They register with a short-lived token and only ever connect out.

tags.name: Webhooks
tags.description: Signed HTTPS requests sent to your own address as things happen, for a repository or a whole workspace.

tags.name: Integrations
tags.description: A workspace's connections to outside systems: the alert sources that open work items (Sentry, Datadog, webhooks) and the issue trackers whose tickets agents read (Jira, Linear).

tags.name: AI
tags.description: A workspace's AI: the AI providers it keeps keys for, managed or self-hosted, and what Ask g1t answers with.

tags.name: Artifacts
tags.description: A workspace's docs, slides, designs and dashboards (Artifacts mode): listing and searching the ones you can open, reading and editing their content in Markdown, making, moving, trashing and restoring them, their versions, and who can open them. Each answers for your own role on it. Not workflow runs' artifacts, which are under Actions. Slides, designs and dashboards answer that they are not here yet.

post.description: Begins a device sign-in. Show the person `verification_uri_complete` and have them open it in a browser, where they sign in or register and approve the code. Then poll `/device/token`.

client_name.description: What is asking, shown to the person approving. For example, Claude Code.

user_code.description: Shown to the person, like WDJB-MJHT.

verification_uri_complete.description: The link to give the person; it carries the code.

post.description: Asks whether the person has approved. Poll no faster than the interval. The token is returned once.

username.description: Lowercased: what the account is found and linked by.

display_username.description: The username as its owner wrote it; the same as username when they chose no case.

verified.description: Whether the account's email is confirmed.

get.description:
Who the access token acts as, and the workspaces it can work in. `kind` is `user` for a person's token, `workspace` for a token that belongs to a workspace, and `agent` for a job's run token.

`token` is what the access token you called with may do: its `scopes` (left out for full access) and `legacy` when it was made before tokens had scopes. A token reaches every workspace and repository whoever it acts as can; its scopes say what it may do there. See [Scopes](/guides/authentication/#scopes). `kind` is `user`, `workspace` for a [workspace access token](/guides/workspaces/#workspace-access-tokens), or `agent` for the token a g1t agent works with. For a workspace token, `username` is the workspace's slug and `workspaces` holds only that workspace. Each workspace carries its `base_permission`: what a member gets on each of its repositories (owners have Admin). Roles given on single repositories are in `grants`, each with `repo_id`, `workspace` and `role`; it is left out when there are none. See [Access and roles](/guides/access-and-roles/).

401.description: A token is required, or the one sent is not valid.

403.description: Signed in, but not allowed to do this: the role you have is not enough, or the token lacks the scope it needs, which `needed_scope` names.

post.description:
Create a workspace. A workspace owns repositories and is the first part of their address: g1t.sh/{workspace}/{repo}. The whoami tool lists the ones you already belong to. A new workspace is free, and each person can own one free workspace: if you already own one (or several, from before), this is refused with `payment_required` (402) until each workspace you own is on the g1t plan or deleted. Workspaces with the plan, an enterprise's terms or a full discount do not count.

`base_permission` is what every member gets on each of its repositories: `read` for a new workspace until an owner changes it with `PATCH /workspaces/{workspace}` or `PUT /workspaces/{workspace}/base_permission`. See [Access and roles](/guides/access-and-roles/). `team_creation` is who may create its teams: `members` (any member) until an owner sets `owners` with `PATCH /workspaces/{workspace}`. A new workspace is free, and each person owns at most one free workspace: while you own one, this answers `402` with `payment_required` and says which, until it is on the plan or deleted. See [One free workspace per person](/guides/usage-and-billing/#one-free-workspace-per-person).

get.description:
One workspace you belong to: its name, description and member count, what every member gets on each of its repositories (base_permission), who may create its teams (team_creation: members or owners), its member privileges (members_can_create_public_repositories, members_can_create_private_repositories, members_can_change_repo_visibility, members_can_delete_repositories, members_can_invite_outside_collaborators), and whether it requires two-factor authentication (two_factor_requirement_enabled). Members only.

`team_creation` is who may create its teams: `members` (any member, the default) or `owners`. The `members_can_…` fields are its [member privileges](/guides/workspaces/#member-privileges), and `two_factor_requirement_enabled` whether it [requires two-factor authentication](/guides/authentication/#require-two-factor-authentication). Change it, and the rest, with [`PATCH /workspaces/{workspace}`](/reference/api/workspaces/update-workspace/). `404` for anyone who is not a member. See [Workspaces](/guides/workspaces/).

delete.description:
Delete a workspace and everything in it. Owners only, signed in as a person, and confirm must be the workspace's slug. Billing must be able to settle it: no unpaid invoice, no prepaid credit left, and no usage this month still being metered; what it owes is charged to its card at once and its plan ends. Its repositories, projects and apps go with it at once, nobody can reach it, and its access tokens stop working. It is kept for 30 days, when g1t's support can restore it as it was; then it is purged, with its webhooks, integrations and workspace secrets. Its statements, invoices and audit log are kept. The slug is never given to another workspace; the person whose username it is may create it again once it is purged. Some workspaces, such as Flagon's, can never be deleted.

Refused with `402` while billing cannot settle it, with a message that says what to do, and with `403` for anyone but an owner signed in as a person, or for a protected workspace. Its repositories, projects and apps go with it; g1t's support can restore it for 30 days. See [Delete a workspace](/guides/workspaces/#delete-a-workspace).

patch.description:
Change a workspace's display name and description, what every member gets on each of its repositories (base_permission: none, read, write or admin), who may create its teams (team_creation: members or owners), its member privileges, and whether it requires two-factor authentication. The member privileges are: members_can_create_public_repositories and members_can_create_private_repositories (who may create each kind; owners always can), members_can_change_repo_visibility (members with the Admin role on a repository may make it public or private), members_can_delete_repositories (they may delete or transfer it) and members_can_invite_outside_collaborators (they may give a role to someone outside the workspace). two_factor_requirement_enabled true holds every member and outside collaborator without two-factor authentication out of the workspace until they turn it on; you need it on yourself first. Only the fields given are changed; give at least one. An empty name falls back to the slug, which this never changes (that is a rename, on Settings); an empty description clears it. Owners only, signed in as a person. Returns the workspace as it is now.

Only the fields given change. `name` is the display name; the slug, the first part of the workspace's addresses, stays as it is. `base_permission` needs the `access:admin` scope as well as `workspace:admin`; [`set_base_permission`](/reference/api/access/set-base-permission/) sets it alone. `team_creation` is `members` (any member may create a team, the default) or `owners`; teams already made stay. The `members_can_…` fields are the workspace's member privileges: who may create public and private repositories, and whether members with the Admin role on a repository may change its visibility, delete or transfer it, and invite outside collaborators. `two_factor_requirement_enabled` holds everyone without two-factor authentication out of the workspace until they turn it on, and needs it on your own account first. Refused with `403` for anyone but an owner signed in as a person. Recorded in the [audit log](/guides/audit-log/). See [Workspaces](/guides/workspaces/).

base_permission.description: What every member gets on each repository: none, read, write or admin. Needs the access:admin scope as well.

team_creation.description: Who may create the workspace's teams: members (any member, the default) or owners (owners only).

members_can_create_public_repositories.description: Members may create public repositories. Owners always can. On by default.

members_can_create_private_repositories.description: Members may create private repositories. Owners always can. On by default.

members_can_change_repo_visibility.description: Members with the Admin role on a repository may make it public or private. On by default; off, only owners can.

members_can_delete_repositories.description: Members with the Admin role on a repository may delete or transfer it. Off by default: only owners can.

members_can_invite_outside_collaborators.description: Members with the Admin role on a repository may give a role on it to someone outside the workspace. On by default; off, only owners can.

two_factor_requirement_enabled.description: Require two-factor authentication of every member and outside collaborator. Those without it keep their place but cannot use the workspace until they turn it on. You need it on yourself first.

get.description:
Your email addresses: each one's `email`, whether it is `verified` (confirmed), `primary` or the `backup`, and when it was added and confirmed. Also whether you keep your address private (`private_email`), your `noreply` address, and `commit_email`, the address on commits g1t makes for you. People only: an agent's or a workspace's token cannot read or change addresses.

Your primary address comes first, then confirmed addresses, then unconfirmed ones. Any confirmed address signs you in, can reset your password and attributes commits to you. See [Email addresses](/guides/authentication/#email-addresses).

post.description:
Add an email address to your account. g1t emails it a link to confirm it; until then it cannot be primary and does not sign you in. Adding an address you added before and have not confirmed sends the link again. An address another account has confirmed cannot be added. An account has at most 10. Needs your account `password`; your confirmed addresses are told. People only.

Answers `403` with code `reauth_required` when `password` is missing or wrong, and `409` when another account has confirmed the address. g1t emails the address a six-digit code and a link; it stays unconfirmed until the code is sent to [`confirm_email`](/reference/api/accounts/confirm-email/) or the link is followed.

post.description:
Confirm an email address with the six-digit `code` from the confirmation email g1t sent it. The same email has a link that does the same; either one works, once, for 60 minutes, and asking for a new email ends both. A new account must confirm its address before it can do anything else: until then this, `GET /user` and `GET /user/emails` are the only calls its token can make, and everything else, MCP included, is refused with `403`. Confirming a new account's address also invites it to the workspace its invite named, when the invite still applies: the answer's `invited_to` names it, and the invitation waits for you to accept or decline it (accept_invitation), or `invite_lapsed` says why not. Ten wrong codes in an hour pause checking for the account. People only.

The code confirms the address it was sent to, and ends the link sent with it. A wrong, used or expired code answers `422` with one message for all three; after ten wrong codes in an hour the account answers `409` for a while, and the link in the email still works. `verified` says whether the account is confirmed: whether its primary address is. `invited_to` is set when the invite the account signed up with brings it into a workspace: confirming the address sends the account an invitation to that workspace, which it accepts with `POST /user/invitations/{id}/accept` or declines; nobody joins a workspace without saying yes. `joined` is kept for older clients and is null. When the invite was revoked or expired, or the workspace deleted, while the account waited, the address is confirmed all the same and `invite_lapsed` says so. See [Confirming your email address](/guides/authentication/#confirming-your-email-address).

delete.description:
Remove an email address from your account. Never your primary address (make another primary first) and never your last confirmed one. Needs your account `password`; every confirmed address, the removed one included, is told. People only.

Give the address in the path, URL-encoded: `DELETE /user/emails/ada.l%40example.org`. Answers `409` for your primary address or your last confirmed one.

patch.description:
Change what your addresses do; only the fields given change. `primary` is a confirmed address to make primary: account mail and password resets go there. `backup` is a confirmed address that also gets security notices, or an empty string for the primary only. Changing either needs your account `password`, and every confirmed address is told. `private_email` keeps your address off commits g1t makes for you (merges and changes made on the web, and agents' commits for you), which use your noreply address instead; `block_private_pushes` refuses pushes whose commits carry one of your addresses while it is private. People only.

Only the fields given change. `primary` and `backup` need `password`; `private_email` and `block_private_pushes` do not.

get.description:
Your invites to g1t, newest first, and how many you have left. Anyone can sign up for g1t without an invite; an invite is a note from you with a link that opens sign-up with your friend's address filled in and confirmed. You have 20 for good (`allowance.limit`, more if g1t granted them): pending and used ones count, and one revoked or expired before it was used comes back. A pending invite's `code` is shown to you; the link is https://g1t.sh/invite/<code>. `status` is `pending`; `awaiting_confirmation` (used to make an account that has not confirmed its address yet); `awaiting_answer` (used to make an account that has yet to accept or decline the workspace it was also invited to); `redeemed` (they joined: `redeemed_by` is their username); `declined`; `expired`; or `revoked`. People only.

Anyone can sign up for g1t without an invite. A revoked or expired invite that was never used is not counted, so it comes back; a used one stays spent. `status` is `pending`, `awaiting_confirmation`, `awaiting_answer` (the account it made has yet to accept or decline the workspace in `workspace`), `redeemed` (they joined, as `redeemed_by`), `declined`, `expired` or `revoked`. See [Invite a friend](/guides/authentication/#invite-a-friend).

401.description: A token is required, or the one sent is not valid.

403.description: Signed in, but not allowed to do this: the role you have is not enough, or the token lacks the scope it needs, which `needed_scope` names.

404.description: It does not exist, or you cannot see it.

post.description:
Invite a friend to g1t by `email`. They get an email from you, with your `message` if you write one, and a link that opens sign-up with their address filled in and confirmed. Their account starts with a workspace of its own. It works for 30 days and uses one of your 20 invites; revoking it before it is used gives it back. Refused with `409` when the address already has a g1t account or you already have a pending invite for it (neither uses one), and `limit` when you have none left. With `workspace`, a workspace you own on a paid plan, they are also invited to it as `role` (`member` unless you give `owner`): once their account is confirmed they accept or decline, and no workspace of their own is made; a free workspace is refused with `payment_required` (402). Returns the invite with its `code`. People only, once your own address is confirmed: an agent's or a workspace's token cannot invite anyone to g1t.

Anyone can read a public repository, which is not listed. `invitations` is empty unless you have the Admin role (`can_manage`). post.description:
Give someone a role on a repository, by username or email address. A member of its workspace gets the role at once (`result` is `granted`, with the `collaborator`). Anyone else becomes an outside collaborator once they accept an invitation, which is emailed to them and waits 7 days (`result` is `invited`, with the `invitation`); an address with no g1t account is sent an invite that makes the account and accepts in one step. The role is read, triage, write, maintain or admin. Needs the Admin role on the repository, signed in as a person with a confirmed email address; agents' and workspaces' tokens are refused. A free workspace can give its members a role, but cannot invite anyone from outside it: that is refused with `payment_required` (402) until the workspace starts the g1t plan.

`invitee` is a username or an email address. A member of the workspace answers `{"result": "granted", "collaborator": {…}}` with the role already given, shown as list_collaborators shows a person. Anyone else answers `{"result": "invited", "invitation": {…}}`: the invitation is emailed and waits 7 days, and the role is theirs once they accept it. An email address without an account gets an invitation with `email` set and `invitee` null, and an invite that makes the account and accepts in one step. Your notifications: one thread for each thing you were told about (a work item, a pull request, a workflow on a branch, a deployment), latest activity first. As in your inbox, only unread threads unless `all` is true; `view` `saved` or `done` lists those instead, read or not. Each thread has a `reason`, why you were told (`agent`, `review_requested`, `assign`, `mention`, `ci_activity`, `security_alert`, `state_change`, `author`, `comment`, `manual` or `subscribed`), a `severity`, the latest activity's `title`, and `count`, how many things have happened on it. Filter by `reason` or `severity`, by `participating` (leaving out what you only watch or subscribed to by hand), by `since` and `before` (RFC 3339, the latest activity), or to one repository. A page holds `per_page` threads, 30 unless you say (at most 100); pass `next` back as `cursor` for the next. Threads about repositories you can no longer read are left out. Your own: a personal access token or a session, never a workspace's.

Unread threads only, unless `all=true`. Threads that wait on you (an agent, or a review asked of you) have severity `warning`.

| `reason` | You were told because |
| --- | --- |
| `agent` | An agent is waiting on you: it asked a question, or g1t stopped until a person steps in |
| `review_requested` | You were asked to review |
| `assign` | You were assigned |
| `mention` | Someone mentioned you by `@username` |
| `ci_activity` | Checks, a workflow or a deployment on your work finished |
| `security_alert` | A security alert on a repository you look after |
| `state_change` | It was closed, reopened or merged |
| `author` | You opened it, or asked g1t for it |
| `comment` | You commented on it |
| `manual` | You subscribed to it by hand |
| `subscribed` | You watch its repository |

With `participating=true`, threads you only follow (`manual`, `subscribed`) are left out. For the next page, pass `next` as `cursor`; `next` is null on the last.

get.description:
What happened across a workspace's repositories that you can read, newest first: pull requests merged, opened and closed, work items opened and closed (linked to the repositories, numbered in the workspace), releases published, deployments that succeeded or failed, pushes (with `default_branch` true for what landed on the default branch without a pull request), reviews, packages, and workflow runs that finished (`workflow`, `run_number`, `conclusion`, `run_id` for workflow get_run, and `production` true for a run of a deploy workflow on the default branch: a repository that deploys itself). Each event has its `kind`, `time`, `repo` (owner/name), `actor` (a username), and where it has them its `number`, `title`, `url` (its page on g1t), `branch`, `commit`, `commits`, `tag` and `error`. `summary` counts merged pull requests, releases, production deployments (projects' production deployments and successful deploy runs on default branches), failed ones, default-branch pushes and failed runs, and in `shipped` the landed commits by where they are. `landed` lists the commits made on default branches in the span, one line each (`repo`, `commit`, `subject`, `author` as git wrote it, `username` when the author's address is a g1t account's, `time`, `url`), and, where the repository deploys, `production`: `live` (a successful deploy carried it, named in `deploy` with its `url`), `deploying`, `failed` (its deploy failed and none since succeeded) or `not_deployed`. That is what shipped: what reached the default branch, and which of it is live. The span is `since` to `until` (RFC 3339; the last 24 hours when `since` is left out, at most 31 days); narrow it with `kinds` (merged, pulls, work_items, releases, deployments, pushes, reviews, comments, packages, runs; all but comments when left out) and `limit` (100 unless you say, at most 200). `complete` is false when more happened than was read: narrow the span or the kinds. For one repository's full timeline use list_events.

What shipped today across a workspace: `since` at the start of the day and `kinds=merged,releases,deployments,pushes,runs`. Each event links to its page on g1t (`url`). `landed` is what reached default branches, each commit with `production` where its repository deploys. Ask g1t reads this to answer questions about a workspace.

Change a project's g1t.page deployment settings; only what you give changes. `enabled: true` turns Deployments on, as Turn on deployments under Settings → Deployments does: production starts building from the default branch at once, and every pull request gets a preview. That needs the g1t plan on the workspace (refused with payment_required otherwise; an owner starts it under Billing), and is refused for a project set to be a library, a tool or other until update_project makes it an app. `enabled: false` takes production and every preview down now and stops building; turning `production` or `previews` off takes those apps down. build_command, output_dir and dockerfile take null or "" to go back to what is found by itself; idle_days is 1 to 90; build_as is auto, static, workers or docker; instance_type is a container size (lite, basic, standard-1 to standard-4). Needs the Admin role on the project's repository. Returns the settings as get_deployment_settings does.

Only the fields given change. `enabled: true` turns Deployments on: production starts building from the default branch at once (an empty repository's first push to it deploys), and every pull request gets a preview. It is refused with `402 payment_required` when the workspace does not have the [g1t plan](/guides/usage-and-billing/#the-g1t-plan), saying where an owner starts it, and with `409 conflict` for a project set to be a library, a tool or other (change `kind` with [`update_project`](/reference/api/projects/update-project/) first). `enabled: false` takes production and every preview down at once. `build_command`, `output_dir` and `dockerfile` given as null or `""` go back to what is found by itself; `idle_days` is 1 to 90; anything else is refused with `422 invalid`. Needs the Admin role on the project's repository (`403` otherwise, saying so) and a token with `repo:admin`. To turn them on as a repository is made, give `deploy: true` to [`create_repo`](/reference/api/repositories/create-repo/). See [Turn on deployments](/guides/deployments/#turn-on-deployments).

get.description:
A workspace's usage over a range of days, at price, and what paid for it. `from` and `until` are UTC days, `YYYY-MM-DD`, with `until` included and at most 400 days in all; left out, the current month so far. `products` narrows it to product families (sandboxes, deployments, git_storage, packages, security, search, other) and `projects` to repositories ("owner/name"). Returns `totals`: `price_micros` less `discount_micros`, `included_micros` and `credits_micros` is `charged_micros`, what is left for the workspace to pay; `pending_micros` is metered this month and charged when it closes, counted in any range that reaches into the current month, and `pending_charged_micros` is what of it will be charged then, after the discount and what g1t covers; `cost_micros` is what it cost g1t. Then `days` (each day and product with usage), `products` (every family, with its meters: quantity, unit, amount, a `daily` amount for each day of the range, any `allowance`, and the split `by_project`), `projects` (every repository with usage in the range), and the credit left now: `credit_micros`, and `ai_credit_micros` for AI credit bought earlier, which still pays toward what is owed. Usage on a meter g1t no longer has, such as agent runs and model requests from before they were retired, is kept on one meter in a last product, `other`, shown only when it has something, so nothing charged is left out. With `group_by` (`product`, `project` or `day`), `groups` adds up the range that way. Amounts are whole millionths of a dollar. Members of the workspace only.

Every product family with meters is listed, in order, even with nothing used; this example shows two. `other` comes last, and only when it has something: usage on meters g1t no longer has, such as agent runs from before they were retired. `daily` has one amount for each day of the range, oldest first. `projects` and `products` take several values separated by commas: `?products=sandboxes,deployments`. A range of more than 400 days, or one that ends before it starts, is refused with `invalid`.

All amounts are whole millionths of a dollar: 500000000 is $500. `max_amount_micros` is null for g1t's own workspaces, which have no ceiling. When `state` is `stopped`, new sandboxes, builds and app requests wait until the limit is raised or the month closes.

A usage invoice's `reason` is `month` (the month closed) or `threshold` (charged near the limit), and its `status` `paid`, `open`, `failed` or `void`. | --- | --- |
| `too_large` | The file is over 3 MB and was ignored. |
| `negation` | A pattern starting with `!`; the line was skipped. |
| `character_range` | A pattern with `[` or `]`; the line was skipped. |
| `bad_pattern` | A pattern that names no path; the line was skipped. |
| `bad_owner` | An owner that is not `@user`, `@workspace/team` or an email address. |
| `bad_section` | A section header that could not be read. |
| `unknown_user` | No account has that username. |
| `unknown_team` | The workspace has no team of that slug. |
| `unknown_email` | No account has confirmed that address. |
| `no_write_access` | The person cannot write to the repository. |

Dismiss an alert with a reason and an optional comment. A secret takes false_positive, used_in_tests, revoked or wont_fix; a dependency takes fix_started, no_bandwidth, tolerable_risk, inaccurate or not_used. A dismissed secret is let through push protection from then on, unless the reason is `revoked`, which marks it fixed. Dismissing either needs the Write role on the repository, or a security manager of its workspace. Returns the alert as it is now. Reopen it with reopen_security_alert.

| Kind | Reasons |
| --- | --- |
| `secret` | `false_positive`, `used_in_tests`, `revoked`, `wont_fix` |
| `dependency` | `fix_started`, `no_bandwidth`, `tolerable_risk`, `inaccurate`, `not_used` |

A reason for the other kind of alert, or one not in the table, is refused with `422`. A secret dismissed as `revoked` becomes `fixed`; with any other reason it becomes `dismissed` and pushes that carry it go through. Dismissing a secret needs the Admin role on the repository; a dependency needs the Write role. A token needs `repo:admin` for either, and a g1t agent’s token never dismisses alerts.

Push past push protection for a blocked secret, with a reason: false_positive or used_in_tests (the alert is closed with that reason) or will_fix_later (it stays open, to be rotated). | `false_positive` | Closed as a false positive |
| `used_in_tests` | Closed as used in tests |
| `will_fix_later` | Stays open, to be rotated |

Upload a SARIF 2.1.0 file: sarif is the file gzipped and base64-encoded; commit_sha the full commit; ref refs/heads/<branch> or refs/pull/<number>/head. For the default branch, new results open alerts and results no longer reported fix theirs. For a pull request, its results new to it on lines it changes become review comments and the Code scanning check, which fails at the repository's threshold. Read at once; the answer says complete or failed and why. Needs the g1t plan on a private repository.

`sarif` is the SARIF 2.1.0 file gzipped, then base64-encoded: `gzip -c results.sarif | base64 -w0`. The upload is read at once: `processing_status` is `complete` or `failed`, with `errors` saying why. For `refs/pull/<number>/head`, the results become the pull request's `Code scanning` check instead of alerts.

Create a repository in one of your workspaces, empty or as a copy of a public git repository elsewhere. It gets a project of its own name; description is that project's. With deploy true, its project's g1t.page Deployments are turned on as soon as it is made, as update_deployment_settings with enabled true does: its first push to the default branch deploys production. When they cannot be turned on (the workspace has no g1t plan, or your role there is below Admin) the repository is still made: `deployments` is null and `deploy_error` says why, and they can be turned on later. Turning them on here needs no scope beyond `repo:create`: you are the new repository's admin.

get.description:
Search all of g1t: repositories (name, their project's description, topics, README), code on default branches (file names and contents), work items, pull requests, people and workspaces. Covers everything public, and private content in workspaces you belong to; signed out, public only. Write words, "exact phrases", -words to leave out, and qualifiers: repo:owner/name, org:workspace, language:rust, path:src/ (a glob with *), is:item, is:pr, is:open, is:closed, is:merged, author:username, label:bug. type picks the kind of results (repositories, code, work items, pull requests or people); without it, the qualifiers decide. Returns one page of results with the matches highlighted, code with line numbers, and how many there are of each kind.

`q` takes words, `"exact phrases"`, `-words` to leave out, and qualifiers: `repo:owner/name`, `org:` (or `workspace:`), `language:`, `path:` (a glob when it has `*`), `is:item`, `is:pr`, `is:open`, `is:closed`, `is:merged`, `is:draft`, `is:public`, `is:private`, `author:` and `label:`; most can be left out with a leading `-`, as in `-label:wontfix`. `type` is `repositories`, `code`, `items`, `pulls` or `people`; without it, `path:` means code, `is:pr` pull requests, `is:item`, `is:open`, `author:` or `label:` work items, and anything else repositories. `counts` says how many results each type has, up to 1,000. Each result's `snippet` (or, for code, each of its `lines`) is a list of parts, `highlight` true where the query matched. Code is searched on default branches and needs a word of three characters or more, unless the query names a `repo:`. Public content is returned to anyone, without a token; private content only to people who can read it (members of its workspace, and people given a role on the repository), checked when the search runs, so a repository made private, or a role taken away, stops appearing at once. A g1t agent's token can search too. A work item or pull request g1t opened has `author` `g1t` and `requested_by` the person it was for; `author:` matches the author.

get.description:
A link to download a branch, tag or commit as a gzipped tar archive (the default branch without ref), good for 10 minutes and needing no token. Over REST, GET …/tarball/{ref} answers 302 with the link in Location, as GitHub does: `curl -L` follows it. Over MCP the link is returned as url, with commit and expires_at. The archive holds one folder, <owner>-<repo>-<first 7 of the commit>/, with executable files and symlinks as git has them and the commit in its pax header. Up to 10,000 files and 24 MB; clone a larger repository. Needs the Read role; a public repository's are open to anyone.

Over REST the answer is `302 Found` with the link in `Location`, as GitHub's is, so `curl -L -H "Authorization: Bearer g1t_…" -o hello.tar.gz https://api.g1t.sh/repos/flagon-io/hello/tarball/main` saves the file and `tar -xzf hello.tar.gz` makes one folder, `flagon-io-hello-7c1e9a4/`; the body above is what the MCP `repository` tool's `tarball` returns. The link is for the commit the ref named when you asked, needs no token and stops working after 10 minutes. `actions/checkout` uses this route in a job container without git.

A branch that is only behind moves forward (fast_forwarded); one with commits of its own gets a merge commit when the two sides' changes do not clash, edits to the same file merging line by line (merged); when both changed the same lines (or one deleted a file the other changed, or both changed a binary file) nothing is changed (conflicted, with the files in conflicts, at most 20): merge the parent's branch in a clone and push, or open a pull request. `status` is `up_to_date`, `fast_forwarded`, `merged` (a merge commit joins the fork's own commits and the parent's) or `conflicted`: both sides changed the files in `conflicts`, and nothing was changed. Merge the parent's branch in a clone and push. Refused with `422` when the repository is not a fork, `403` without the Write role on it, and `404` when its parent is gone or you can no longer read it. patch.description:
Change how a repository handles pull requests, commits and work items. Only the fields given are changed; required_checks replaces the whole list. At least one merge method must stay allowed, and default_merge_method must be one of them. A custom commit message (merge_commit_message or squash_commit_message custom) uses its template, whose {title}, {number}, {body}, {branch}, {head_repo}, {base}, {author}, {commits}, {items} and {co_authors} are filled in; pull_title_and_commits is for squash commits only. The branch protection fields (required_checks, require_up_to_date, required_approvals, count_agent_approvals, allow_ignoring_checks, merge_queue, require_code_owner_review) are written to the repository's "Default branch protection" ruleset, made when it has none; rules only rulesets have stay as they are. A required check is named as list_check_names gives it: a workflow's name, such as CI, or another status's context, such as g1t / deploy. Needs the Maintain role or higher, and the Admin role to change a branch protection field.

`required_checks` replaces the whole list: at most 20 names, each a workflow's name or another status's context, as [`list_check_names`](/reference/api/repositories/list-check-names/) gives them. A pull request merges only once each passes on its head; one nothing has reported holds it too. With the merge queue on, each must also pass on the queued state, so the workflows behind them need `merge_group` in their `on:`. `required_approvals` is at most 6. See [Required checks](/guides/checks/#required-checks). With `require_code_owner_review`, a pull request into the default branch merges only once the code owners of every file it changes have approved it, as many as each section of its CODEOWNERS file asks: see [Code owners](/guides/codeowners/). At least one of `allow_merge_commit`, `allow_squash_merge`, `allow_rebase_merge` and `allow_fast_forward` stays on, and `default_merge_method` must be one of them (`422` otherwise). `merge_commit_template` and `squash_commit_template` are used with `custom`: see [Commit messages](/guides/pull-requests/#commit-messages) for their placeholders. `has_work_items` `null` goes back to the default: on for a repository, off for a fork. See [Repository settings](/guides/managing-repositories/#settings).

auto_merge.description: Land a pull request without a person once every rule is met.

required_checks.description: The checks that must pass on a pull request's head before it merges into the default branch, by name: a workflow's name (CI) or another status's context (g1t / deploy). list_check_names gives the names seen lately. Replaces the whole list; an empty list requires none.

require_up_to_date.description: Refuse to merge a pull request that is behind the default branch. When false, merging brings it up to date first.

required_approvals.description: How many approving reviews a merge needs.

count_agent_approvals.description: Whether approvals by g1t (@g1t) count towards required_approvals.

allow_ignoring_checks.description: Whether someone who may merge can bypass required checks that have not passed, with ignore_checks.

merge_queue.description: Merge through a queue: each pull request is tested together with those ahead of it, and only a combination that passed reaches the default branch.

require_code_owner_review.description: Refuse to merge until the code owners of every file a pull request changes, as the CODEOWNERS file of the branch it merges into names them, have approved it, as many as each section asks. Only people's approvals count, and g1t's only where the file names @g1t.

allow_merge_commit.description: Let pull requests merge with a merge commit (merge). At least one method stays allowed.

allow_squash_merge.description: Let pull requests merge as one squashed commit (squash).

allow_rebase_merge.description: Let pull requests merge by making each of their commits again on the base (rebase).

allow_fast_forward.description: Let pull requests merge by moving the base to their head, with no new commit (fast_forward). Off unless turned on.

default_merge_method.description: The method offered first, and used when a merge names none. Must be allowed.

merge_commit_message.description: What a merge commit says unless its merger writes it: default ("Merge pull request #12 from owner/branch" and its title), pull_title (its title, with its number), pull_title_and_description (and its description below), or custom (merge_commit_template).

squash_commit_message.description: What a squash commit says unless its merger writes it: default (its title for one commit, else its title and the commits' messages), pull_title, pull_title_and_description, pull_title_and_commits (its title, and each commit's message below), or custom (squash_commit_template).

merge_commit_template.description: With merge_commit_message custom: the message, its first line the title. {title}, {number}, {body}, {branch}, {head_repo}, {base}, {author}, {commits}, {items} and {co_authors} are filled in. An empty string clears it.

squash_commit_template.description: With squash_commit_message custom: the message, with the same placeholders as merge_commit_template. An empty string clears it.

suggest_updating_branches.description: Offer to update a pull request's branch whenever its base has new commits, not only when it must be up to date to merge.

allow_auto_merge.description: Let people turn on auto-merge for a pull request, so it merges on its own once everything it needs is met.

delete_branch_on_merge.description: Delete a pull request's branch once it merges. It can be restored from the pull request.

require_web_commit_sign_off.description: Commits made on g1t (web edits, merge and squash commits) carry a Signed-off-by: trailer for whoever made them.

allow_commit_comments.description: Let anyone who can read the repository comment on its commits. Existing comments stay readable either way.

auto_close_items.description: Land the work items a pull request names (its item, and Fixes #12 in its title or description) in this repository when it merges into the default branch, closing those with nothing left to land; and the same for commits pushed there.

has_work_items.description: Whether work items can be filed from it (with it as their origin). null goes back to the default: on for a repository, off for a fork. Work items filed from it before stay readable either way, and it can always be linked as a target.

post.description:
Report a check run on a commit: name and head_sha are required; status (queued, in_progress or completed; queued by default), conclusion (success, failure, neutral, cancelled, skipped, timed_out or action_required; it makes the run completed), started_at and completed_at (RFC 3339; filled in when left out), details_url (your page for it), external_id (your id for it), output (title, summary and text in Markdown, and up to 50 annotations: path, start_line, end_line, start_column, end_column, annotation_level notice, warning or failure, message, title, raw_details) and actions (up to 3 buttons: label, description, identifier). app names who reports it, by default your token's name. Runs are grouped per reporter and commit into a check suite. A check run is a check: a required check of its name is met by it, a cancelled one failing. Needs the Write role; publishes check_run.created, and check_run.completed when it is created completed.

Start a run as `queued` or `in_progress` and complete it later with [`update_check_run`](/reference/api/checks/update-check-run/), or create it completed. `app` names who reports it; by default it is your token's name, and a g1t Actions job's `G1T_TOKEN` reports as g1t Actions. Each reporter's runs on a commit form one check suite. The run also stands as a status of its name, so a required check `lint` is met by it: `success`, `neutral` and `skipped` pass, any other conclusion fails. See the [Checks guide](/guides/checks/).

Every rule that holds for a branch (or a tag, with target tag) of a repository, from every ruleset that targets it, the repository's and its workspace's: each with its type, parameters and applies_to, and the ruleset_id, ruleset_name, level and enforcement it comes from. Active rules come first, then those of rulesets in evaluate. rulesets lists the rulesets with who may bypass each. A branch name with slashes is URL-encoded in the path.

A branch with slashes in its name is URL-encoded as one segment: `/rules/branches/release%2F1.x`. Add `?target=tag` for a tag.

Takes the Write role.

A `fail` of a ruleset in `evaluate` is what it would have refused. Pass `next` as `before` for the next page. `insights` counts the last 30 days.

List a repository's deployments wherever they run, newest first: those reported through this API, those g1t Actions made for jobs with an `environment:`, and g1t.page builds (production and previews). Each has its environment, ref and sha, task, description, payload, transient_environment and production_environment, its latest state (queued, in_progress, success, failure, error or inactive), environment_url and log_url, creator, and source (api, actions or g1t_page), with run_id and run_url for g1t Actions and project and number for g1t.page. See [Deployments API](/guides/deployments-api/).

post.description:
Report a deployment of a commit to an environment, from any CI or script. ref is the branch, tag or commit deployed; sha is resolved from it unless you give the whole commit id. environment is production unless you say (any name up to 255 characters, such as staging or review/feature-x; names are matched without regard to case, and the first spelling is kept). task is deploy unless you say; payload is any JSON object, returned as given. production_environment is true for an environment named production unless you say; transient_environment marks one that goes away, such as a review app. Its first status is state (queued unless you say), with environment_url and log_url. Each status also shows on the commit as the check `deploy / <environment>`, which a ruleset's required_deployments rule can require. Needs the Write role. Returns the deployment with its statuses.

Report from any CI with an access token that has `deployments:write` (the CI preset has it) and the Write role. Then report each step with [`POST …/deployments/{id}/statuses`](/reference/api/deployments/create-deployment-status/). Each status sets the check `deploy / <environment>` on the commit. A g1t Actions job with an `environment:` does all of this itself. See [Deployments API](/guides/deployments-api/).

post.summary: Start a g1t.page build from a workflow
post.description:
From a running g1t Actions job, open a g1t.page build of one of the repository's projects, which the job then builds in its own checkout with `g1t-runner deploy` (the g1t/deploy action does both). Only the job's own token (G1T_TOKEN) may call it, with `deployments: write` (or `pages: write`) in its `permissions:`. project is the project's slug; it may be left out when the repository has one project with Deployments on. The run decides what is built: a run on the project's production branch (a push, a dispatch or a schedule there) builds production, a pull request's run builds that pull request's preview, and a run on another branch builds that branch's preview; a tag's run is refused. sha is the commit built, the run's unless you say. A pull request from a fork or from someone without the Write role, and a run that had to be approved, get no build secrets. The workspace's plan must include Deployments and its spend limit must not be reached; the build's time is the job's Actions time and is not charged again. Returns deploy_id and token (DEPLOY_ID and DEPLOY_TOKEN for `g1t-runner deploy`, the token good for this build alone until it finishes), kind (production or preview), project, branch, number, commit, url (the app's address), trusted, the project's root_dir, build_command and output_dir, build_as (auto, static, workers or docker) and dockerfile (its Dockerfile's path, or null to find `Dockerfile` or `Containerfile`), and build_env and build_secrets (the project's variables and secrets for builds of that kind). The commit's `g1t / deploy` check is pending until the build reports.

Called from a workflow step with the job's own token, `${{ github.token }}`, in a job with `permissions: deployments: write`; the [`g1t/deploy`](/guides/deployments/#deploying-from-a-workflow) action calls it, masks the token and the secrets, and runs `g1t-runner deploy` with them. Any other token is refused. This is a pull request's run, so it builds the pull request's preview; the same workflow on the production branch builds production. See [Deploying from a workflow](/guides/deployments/#deploying-from-a-workflow).

put.summary: Create or update an environment's protection rules
put.description:
Create an environment's protection rules, or change them; fields left out stay as they are. A job that names the environment with `environment:` waits, once its needs are done, until the rules let it through, and only then gets the environment's secrets. reviewers: up to 6, each {"type": "User" or "Team", "name": a username or a team's slug} (id is read as the name too); a job waits until one of them approves it. prevent_self_review: whoever started the run may not approve it. wait_timer: minutes each job waits, 0 to 43200. deployment_branch_policy: null lets every branch deploy; {"protected_branches": true} only branches the repository's rules protect (the default branch included); {"custom_branch_policies": true} only the branches and tags in branch_policies, each {"name": a pattern such as release/*, "type": "branch" or "tag"}. can_admins_bypass (true unless you say): admins may approve without being reviewers, which also skips the wait. The environment's name is up to 40 letters, digits, - and _, matched without regard to case. Needs the Admin role. Returns the environment with its protection_rules.

Fields left out stay as they are. A job with `environment: production` now waits for syntaqx or someone in deployers to approve it, then ten minutes, and runs only on a protected branch.

get.description:
The timeline of a repository: pushes, its work items, pull requests, comments, sessions, claims and integration results, newest first; page back with before. To follow it, give after (an event id): the events written after that one come oldest first, and the last one's id is the next call's after. With after and wait (seconds, at most 25), a call that finds nothing holds on until a matching event is written or the wait ends, then returns what it has, perhaps nothing. Narrow it with types, numbers (work items and pull requests, matching events about them and comments on them), since and limit (50 by default, at most 200).

Returns 50 events a page, newest first. To page back, send the `id` of the last event you have as `before`. `actor` is a user id, and `data` depends on `type`.

To follow a repository without a webhook, send `after` instead: the events written after that event come oldest first, and the last one's `id` is your next `after`. Add `wait` (seconds, at most 25) and a call that finds nothing holds on until a matching event is written or the time is up, then returns what it has, which may be an empty list; call again with the same `after`. Events come in the order g1t wrote them, so none is skipped when two arrive close together.

```sh
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $G1T_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.g1t.sh/repos/acme/rocket/events?after=evt_01m43smh3ve52vkcna207vqctf&types=work.claimed,integration.failed&numbers=12&wait=25"
```

`types` and `numbers` are comma-separated lists in a query string, arrays in a body or an MCP call. `numbers` matches events about those work items and pull requests (`data.number`) and comments, reviews and links on them (`data.item`). `since` is an RFC 3339 time. `after` and `before` cannot be given together.

A workspace's work items, newest first. A work item is any tracked work (a feature, a bug, a chore) of the workspace, numbered in its sequence with new pull requests, and linked to the repositories it concerns: its `origin` (where it was filed, if it was filed in one), its `target`s (where the work is meant to land) and those it `touched` (where a pull request or commit for it landed or is under way). Filter by state, by a label's name, by a milestone's number, by assignee, and with repo by a repository it is linked to (role narrows it to one kind of link). With horizon, only the open work items on that horizon of the plan, in the plan's order: urgent first, then by rank (triage newest first). limit is how many, 1 to 100 (100 if left out). With parent, only the sub-items of the work item of that number; with project (a slug), only those in that project. Each work item says the `project` it is in (its id, slug, name, color and icon), and where it stands in the plan: `horizon`, `appetite`, `budget_usd`, `urgent` and `planned_at`; and `parent`, the number of the work item it is a sub-item of, and with sub-items `sub_item_progress` (`done` of `total` closed). Members see every work item; anyone who can read a repository sees the work items filed in it.

Returns at most 100 work items (limit takes fewer), newest first; with horizon, the open ones on that horizon in the plan's order. Each lists the repositories it is linked to in `repos`, with its role in each. `comment_count` counts comments, not events such as "opened #14 for this".

A work item: its description (which may say what done means, under "Definition of done"), labels, milestone, `repos` (each linked repository with its `role`, its `legacy_number` when it was filed there as an issue before work items, and whether the work `landed` there), `resolutions` (what landed it in each repository: a merged pull request, or a commit pushed to its default branch, with who pushed it), its comments and reactions, every pull request made for it, in any repository, and `parent` and `sub_items` (each with its `number`, `title` and `state`), as far as you can see them. Read this before opening a pull request, to see what others have already tried. A comment one of the workspace's agents wrote as itself has `agent` (its `id`, `handle`, `display_name` and `avatar_seed`) and `acting_for` (the person it acted for, whose access capped it); its `author` is the agent, of kind `agent`. The workspace is `workspace`, its slug; with only `repo`, the repository's workspace.

A closed work item says how it was closed: `reason` is `completed` or `not_planned`, and `resolutions` says what landed it in each repository: `pull`, the pull request whose merge did it, or `commit`, the commit pushed to the default branch whose message did (`Fixes #12`), with `pushed_by` saying who pushed it. `repos` lists the repositories it is linked to, with `landed` true where the work landed. Each pull request made for it is listed, in any repository; one closed because another was merged has `superseded_by` set.

post.description:
Close a work item without a pull request. A work item closes by itself once what closes it has landed in every target: a pull request whose title or description names it after a closing keyword (Fixes #12) merging into a repository's default branch, or such a commit pushed there, marks that repository landed. When a commit already on a default branch did the work, give it as commit, with repo the repository it is in: it lands there as its push would have, and the work item closes if nothing else is left to land. A commit that is not on the default branch, or whose message does not name the work item after a closing keyword, is refused with `422`; a work item already closed, with `409`. A work item with open sub-items is never closed with them silently: without sub_items it is refused with `409`, naming them; sub_items leave leaves them open, close closes them too (with the same reason, and their own open sub-items), and move makes them sub-items of move_to. A commit closing it leaves them. Closing the last open sub-item leaves its parent open, and says so on the parent. Its author may close their own work item, as may the person g1t filed one for; anyone else needs the Triage role. The workspace is `workspace`, its slug; with only `repo`, the repository's workspace.

With `commit` and `repo`, a commit already on that repository's default branch whose message names the work item after a closing keyword (`Fixes #12`), it lands there as pushing it would have: a resolution is recorded, the event is `work_item.landed` (and `work_item.closed` with `resolutions` once nothing else is left to land), and the timeline says "landed this in" the commit, linked. Give `commit` as its full hash. A commit not on the default branch, or one whose message does not name the work item, is refused (`422`); a work item already closed is `409`, saying what closed it. See [Closing work items](/guides/pull-requests/#closing-work-items).

Every open work item is on one horizon: triage (not placed yet; where new ones start), now (what the workspace is on), next (ranked: the top is taken next), later (wanted, not ranked yet) or set_aside (out of every view but search). Only the fields given change. horizon moves it, last there unless a position is given; before or after (another open work item's number) puts it next to that one, on that one's horizon; top puts it first on its horizon. Give at most one of before, after and top; triage takes none, since it is in the order work items came in. appetite (small, medium or large) is how much the work is worth and budget_usd what an agent on it may spend (in dollars, above 0 and up to 100000); null clears either. urgent true puts it first in Now, ahead of its rank, until it closes. Needs the Triage role on the work item; moving it into or out of Now, ranking it within Now, and urgent need the Write role through workspace membership, the right to manage milestones. A closed work item is refused with `409`. Returns the work item. A work_item.planned event, with horizon, from_horizon when it moved, appetite and urgent.

Moves #12 into Now, just after #9, and says it is small. Give at most one of before, after and top; with none, a new horizon puts it last there and the same horizon leaves it where it is. appetite and budget_usd take null to clear them. A work_item.planned event says where it is now (`horizon`), where it was (`from_horizon`, when it moved), its `appetite` and whether it is `urgent`.

get.description:
A workspace's plan, as you may see it: `now` in full (urgent first, then by rank, at most 100) with `now_cap`, how many Now holds before the plan says it is over; `next` by rank, its top 10 (with all, up to 100) and `next_total`; then counts only: `triage_total`, `later_total` with `later` grouped by the repository each is filed in (`repo` "owner/name", none for those filed in the workspace; the largest 50 groups), and `set_aside_total`. With repo, only work items linked to it. Members see every work item; anyone who can read a repository sees those filed in it. list_work_items with horizon lists one horizon, such as Later or Triage, in the plan's order.

Now is urgent first, then by rank; Next is its top 10 unless all is given, and next_total says how many it holds. Triage, Later and Set aside are counts only: list_work_items with horizon lists them, in the plan's order, at most 100 at a time. A Later group with repo null holds the work items filed in the workspace, not in a repository. progress says how each in Now stands: its hill (figuring_out, decided, building or landing, from its decisions, commits and pull requests), when anything last happened on it, quiet after 5 days with nothing, and standing, a sentence or two g1t drafts from its record with the workspace's AI provider (null without one). landed is what closed from Now in the last 7 days; triage_waiting counts work items in Triage for more than 7 days; set_aside_recent, those set aside in the last 30 days (g1t sets aside work items untouched for 90 days in Later). A work item in Triage carries suggestion: where g1t suggests it goes (horizon, appetite, duplicate_of, why).

patch.summary: Tick a box of a work item's task list
patch.description:
Tick or untick a box of a work item's task list: the `- [ ]` and `- [x]` items of its body, numbered from 1 in the order they are written (boxes in fenced code blocks are examples, not boxes). Name the box by task, its number, or by text, words of it: the box whose text is exactly that, ignoring case and spacing, else the one box whose text contains it; text more than one box has is refused with `422`, naming them. checked is true (the default) to tick it and false to untick it. Only that box changes, and it is changed in the body as it is at that moment, so a box someone else ticked meanwhile is kept. With task, give expected, the box's text as you read it: when a box was added or removed above it since, the one box with that text is ticked instead, and when none or several have it the call is refused with `409` rather than ticking the wrong box. A box already as asked is left as it is (changed false). Returns the box (number, line, text, checked), whether it changed, the body after, and how many boxes are done of the total. Whoever may edit the body may: its author, the person g1t filed it for, or anyone with the Triage role. A change is a work_item.updated event. The workspace is `workspace`, its slug; with only `repo`, the repository's workspace.

With text instead of task ("announce"), the box whose text says it. Ticking a box someone ticked already answers changed false and leaves the body as it is.

get.description:
Everything about a work item an agent needs before working on it, in one call: the `item`, its `definition_of_done` (the items under its "Definition of done" heading); `repos`, each repository it is linked to (origin, targets, touched) with its `role`, whether the work `landed` there, the `required_checks` every pull request into its default branch must pass, and its `pulls` for the work item, each with its status, required checks as they stand on its head, whether it merges cleanly, the other pull requests it overlaps and its place in the merge queue; `missing`, the targets it has not landed in yet; `suggested_targets`, repositories of the workspace it may belong in, likeliest first, each with `why` (link_work_item with role target confirms one); active `claims`; `sessions` on it or its pull requests; `blocked_by` (each work item it waits on, with claims and pull requests) and `blocks` (the work items waiting on it); `decisions` recorded about it; `last_integration_failure`; and `recent`, its latest coordination events, newest first.

`repos` are the repositories it is linked to (origin, targets, touched), each with `landed`, the `required_checks` of its default branch and its `pulls` for the work item, oldest first; `required_checks`, `mergeable`, `overlaps` and `queue` (its `state` and `position` in the merge queue, 1 at the front) are filled in for those still open or draft. `missing` lists the targets it has not landed in yet, and `suggested_targets` the repositories of the workspace it may belong in, each with `why`: link one as a target with link_work_item. `recent` holds up to 20 coordination events about the work item or its pull requests, newest first. post.description:
Claim an open work item: say you are working on it. A claim is advisory, never a lock: anyone may claim a work item someone else has, and `others` lists the claims already on it, so you can coordinate or pick something else. It lasts `ttl_minutes` (30 unless you say, up to 240) and is renewed by claiming again or, when you give the `session_id` of one of your sessions, by that session's heartbeats. Name the work item by `workspace` and `number`; `repo`, the repository of your checkout, names the workspace when `workspace` is left out and says where the claim is made from. Returns your `claim`, the `others`, and `blocked_by`: each work item this one waits on, with its claims and pull requests. A new claim is a work.claimed event; one taking over a hand-off says which in `took_over`. For work that has no work item yet, leave out `number` and give `title` (and `body`): the work item is opened first (filed from `repo` when given; a work_item.opened event), then claimed, the session named by `session_id` is attached to it, and `item` is the work item opened. The session is checked first, so a claim it would refuse opens nothing.

A claim is advisory: it is made even when `others` lists someone already on the work item. Claiming a work item you hold renews your claim. Refused with `409` for a closed work item. See [Claims](/work/claims-and-dependencies/#claims).

post.description:
Start a session: one run of your own harness (a Claude Code session, a Codex run) on a repository, so others can see who is working on what. `harness` is claude_code, codex, cursor, copilot or other. Give `harness_session_id`, the harness's own id for the session, and starting again with it returns the session already started (refreshing the work item, pull request, branch, title and head given) instead of a new one, so a hook that fires twice is harmless. `item` and `pull` attach it to a work item of the repository's workspace and a pull request of the repository; a pull request for a work item attaches that work item too. A subagent is a session of its own: give `parent_id` (one of your sessions here), its `agent_type`, the `task` and `prompt` its parent gave it, and as `harness_session_id` the parent's harness id, `/agent/` and the subagent's id; it starts on the parent's work item, pull request and branch unless it says otherwise, sees and is seen by its siblings in get_work and list_sessions, and once ended stays ended when started again. Returns the session (`id` `ses_…`, `state` active, idle or ended). A new session, or one started again after it ended, is a session.started event. Needs a confirmed email address and a role that may open work items.

Idempotent on `harness_session_id`: a second start with it returns this session, so call it from a hook without checking first. `state` is `active`, `idle` (no heartbeat for 15 minutes) or `ended` (ended, or no heartbeat for 30 minutes: `end_reason` `timed_out`). A subagent gives `parent_id`, `agent_type`, `task` and `prompt`. See [Sessions](/guides/sessions/).

patch.description:
Update one of your sessions: attach it to a work item or pull request, or change its branch, head commit or title. Only the fields given change. An empty body is a heartbeat: every call keeps the session active and renews the claims made from it. A session reads as idle after 15 minutes without one and ends (`end_reason` timed_out) after 30 minutes; a heartbeat brings a timed-out one back. Attaching a pull request moves the entries recorded so far into that pull request's session. A subagent's `task`, `prompt`, `model` and `result` (what it reported, up to 8,000 characters) can be set too; a subagent that ended takes them and stays ended. `usage` reports the session's token usage so far, per model, replacing what was reported before: g1t estimates `cost_usd` from it at Anthropic's list price (none when no model in it has a known price), with `cost_partial` true when some of it was for a model it has no price for. Returns the session; one ended with end_session is refused with `409`.

Send `{}` as a heartbeat. Each call renews the session's claims and brings back one that timed out. `usage` is the session's whole usage so far, so each report replaces the last; `cost_usd` is estimated from it at Anthropic's list price. See [Sessions](/guides/sessions/#what-a-session-cost). Refused with `404` for a session that is not yours, and `409` for one you ended.

post.description:
Record entries in one of your sessions: up to 200 at a time, each with `kind` (prompt, message, tool_call, tool_result, note, or skill for a skill it used, by name), `text` (up to 64,000 characters), and for tools `tool`. Give each a `key` and recording it again does nothing, so a retried hook records it once. `touched` says what it touched, up to 200: `{ kind, value }` with kind file (a path from the repository's root), commit, branch, pull (one it opened) or item (a work item it named); each is kept once, ties the session to the pull requests and work items it names, and a file another active session touched too (outside its own parents and subagents, so siblings yes) is an overlap.detected event for both, once per pair and again when a file it was not announced for joins. Entries of a session attached to a pull request show in that pull request's session too, where reviewers read why the change is what it is. `acknowledge` accepts up to 100 exact pending update IDs this session has considered; reading alone never acknowledges. Recording is a heartbeat. Returns how many were `recorded`, how many were `duplicates`, and how many of the `acknowledge` IDs were `acknowledged` (fewer than given means some were not this session's updates).

Up to 200 entries a request. An entry whose `key` the session recorded before is counted in `duplicates` and not recorded again. Entries of a session on a pull request show in that pull request's session too (read_session). `acknowledge` (up to 100 update IDs from get_session's `updates`) clears those updates for this session only; `acknowledged` counts the IDs that were this session's.

A variable's row can become a secret this way; a secret never becomes a variable. `brokered_hosts` brokers the secret: workflow jobs on g1t's machines get a stand-in in place of its value, and g1t puts the real value on the job's requests to those hosts (in headers, Basic auth included, and the query string) as they leave its sandbox, so the value never enters it; a self-hosted runner whose jobs run on Linux or macOS passes the job's requests to those hosts through g1t, so the value never reaches its computer either. Keys are uppercased. See [secrets and variables](/guides/secrets-and-variables/).
