put.summary: Set a secret for a workspace
put.description: Add or change a secret's row. Without `id` or `environments`, the key's row for every environment, as GitHub's API addresses a secret. `available_to` is workflows and/or deployments (both, for a new row); `environments` limits it to some, such as production or preview, so a key can hold a value per environment. A variable's row can become a secret this way; a secret never becomes a variable. `brokered_hosts` brokers the secret: workflow jobs on g1t's machines get a stand-in in place of its value, and g1t puts the real value on the job's requests to those hosts (in headers, Basic auth included, and the query string) as they leave its sandbox, so the value never enters it; a self-hosted runner whose jobs run on Linux or macOS passes the job's requests to those hosts through g1t, so the value never reaches its computer either. A brokered secret is read by workflows only and its value is at least 8 characters; an empty list stops brokering it. A repository's need the Admin role on it; a workspace's, an owner. Workspace tokens, G1T_TOKEN included, cannot change them.

Upload an image to show in a work item's or a pull request's description or in a comment: a screenshot of a preview, say, instead of committing it to the repository. data is the file base64-encoded, name its file name (the image's alt text), content_type optional (checked against the bytes). PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP of at most 10 MB; a larger file is refused with 413 too_large, another type (SVG, PDF, anything its bytes do not show to be one of those) with 415 unsupported_type. Anyone who may comment on the repository may. Returns its id, url (on the usercontent origin, g1tusercontent.com on g1t.sh), name, size, content_type, and markdown (`![name](url)`) to paste into the body or summary of open_work_item, update_work_item, add_work_item_comment, add_comment, create_pull_request or mark_pull_request_ready. Its address is its permission: anyone given it can see the image, even one from a private repository. Over MCP the file travels in the tool call, so keep it small (a few hundred KB); `g1t attach FILE` uploads one from disk and prints the markdown.

`data` is the file base64-encoded: `base64 -w0 preview.png`. Paste `markdown` into the `body` of a work item, pull request or comment, or a pull request's `summary`. The type is read from the bytes; a file over 10 MB is refused with `413` (`too_large`), one that is not a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP with `415` (`unsupported_type`). From a shell, `g1t attach preview.png` does all of it and prints the markdown.

post.description:
Start a change. Opens a draft pull request with its own fork of the repository and returns the fork's git remote. Clone it, commit your work there, push, record your session as you go, then call mark_pull_request_ready. Give item, the number of the work item it is for in the repository's workspace, whenever there is one; this repository is then linked to it as touched, if it was not a target already. If the change is already on a branch pushed to the repository, give that branch instead: no fork is made and the pull request is ready for review at once. It merges into the default branch unless base names another existing branch; leave base out unless you were asked for another.

`title` defaults to the work item's title, and is required when there is no `item`. Opening one for a work item links this repository to it as touched, unless it is a target already. Push to `git.remote` with your username and an access token as the password.

Send `branch` to open the pull request from a branch already pushed to the repository. No fork is made, `fork` is `null`, `git.remote` is the repository itself, and the pull request is `open` at once.

get.description:
A pull request's status, base (the branch it merges into), head commit, labels, milestone, comments and reviews, the work item it is for (`item`), its checks (statuses: what each workflow run reported on its head, with a link to the run; get_workflow_run and get_job_logs say why one failed), required_checks (each check the rules of the branch it merges into require, as success, failure, pending or expected when nothing has reported it yet), rules (each rule of that branch it does not meet yet, with the ruleset it comes from, what is wrong and how to meet it, in `unmet`; those you may bypass in `bypassable`; those of rulesets in evaluate that would refuse it in `evaluate`; and whether merging joins the merge queue), whether it is behind the branch it would merge into, and overlaps: other pull requests in progress that change the same files. An overlap with a pull request for a different work item means the two will conflict; say so, or keep clear of those files. `pull.reviewers` lists the people asked to review it and `pull.team_reviewers` the teams, as `workspace/team`. `code_owners` is there when the branch it merges into has a CODEOWNERS file: its `path`, whether code owners' approval is `required`, `reviews` (one per section and rule that owns a changed file, with its `section`, `line`, `pattern`, `owners`, `files`, whether it is `optional`, the approvals `required`, who it was `approved_by` and `changes_requested_by`, and whether it is `satisfied`), what is still `missing`, and how many `errors` the file has (get_codeowners_errors lists them). A comment one of the workspace's agents wrote as itself has `agent` (its `id`, `handle`, `display_name` and `avatar_seed`) and `acting_for` (the person it acted for, whose access capped it); its `author` is the agent, of kind `agent`. An agent's review also has `advisory: true`: its `verdict` (none, for a review that only comments) is shown but never counts toward required approvals or code owners, and never blocks a merge.

| Field | |
| --- | --- |
| `pull.files` | The files it changes, with lines added and removed. |
| `statuses` | Its checks: what each workflow run (or another tool, such as a deployment) reported on its head, as `pending`, `success`, `failure` or `error`, with a link to the run. |
| `required_checks` | Each check the default branch requires (see [`update_repo_settings`](/reference/api/repositories/update-repo-settings/)), as it stands on the head: `success`, `failure`, `pending`, or `expected` when nothing has reported it yet. It merges only once all are `success`. |
| `checks` | Set when the merge queue took it out, with why in `error`. Older pull requests may show a run of commands from their work item here, from before checks were workflows. |
| `overlaps` | Other pull requests in progress that change the same files. |
| `behind` | Whether the default branch has moved since it was made. |
| `landing` | Whether it is being brought up to date to land. |
| `lifecycle` | For a pull request g1t is seeing through: its stage, such as `working`, `checking`, `reviewing` or `needs_you`. |
| `comments` | Comments, reviews and events, with `path`, `line` and `verdict`. |
| `messages` | Messages sent to the agent working on it. |
| `pull.reviewers`, `pull.team_reviewers` | The people asked to review it, `g1t` among them when a g1t agent was, and the teams, as `workspace/team`. Change them with [`request_reviewers`](/reference/api/pull-requests/request-reviewers/). |
| `code_owners` | Present when the branch it merges into has a CODEOWNERS file: its `path`, whether code owners' approval is `required` there, `reviews` (one per section and rule that owns a changed file: `section`, `line`, `pattern`, `owners`, `files`, `optional`, the approvals `required`, `approved_by`, `changes_requested_by` and `satisfied`), what is still `missing`, as the merge box says it, and how many `errors` the file has; [`get_codeowners_errors`](/reference/api/repositories/get-codeowners-errors/) lists them. |
| `mergeable` | Whether it merges cleanly into its target: `clean`, `conflicting`, `checking` (being worked out) or `unknown`. Worked out ahead of time whenever it or its target moves. |
| `conflicts` | When `mergeable` is `conflicting`, the files that conflict. Resolve them by merging the target in, or have g1t do it. |
| `earlier_checks` | Earlier records like `checks`, newest first. |

Checks are the repository's workflows: they run on `pull_request` events when it is opened, marked ready and pushed to. Read why one failed with [`get_workflow_run`](/reference/api/actions/get-workflow-run/) and [`get_job_logs`](/reference/api/actions/get-job-logs/).

patch.description:
Change a pull request: its title and body (its description; empty takes it away); item, the number of its own work item in the repository's workspace (null or 0 takes it away); base, the branch it merges into (an existing branch; needs the Write role or higher); its labels (the workspace's labels, replacing the set); its milestone (a number, or null or 0 for none; needs the Triage role); and assignees and reviewers (each replacing the set). Only the fields given change, and a field this action does not take is refused with `422` rather than ignored. Its author, or whoever asked g1t for it, may change it; anyone else needs the Triage role or higher, and the Write role for its title, body or item. A new title or body is read again for the work items it closes (Fixes #12) and is part of (Part of #12), as when it opened: those it no longer names are dropped, those it newly names are added if both you and its author may see them, and its own work item stays first. Its item changes only if you can see both the work item it had and the one it gets, which must be open. A merged or closed pull request's title and body can still change, and nothing else: a merged one keeps the work items it landed. A change to its title, body or item is a pull.edited event, with changes saying what each was. A new base is a pull.base_changed event: it leaves the merge queue, and whether it is behind, merges cleanly and has the checks it needs is worked out against the new base. state open reopens a closed pull request, as reopen_pull_request does, before anything else changes; state closed closes it, as close_pull_request does, after.

Only the fields given change; one it does not take is refused with 422. A new title or body is read again for the work items it closes and is part of. A merged or closed pull request takes only title and body, and a merged one keeps what it landed. A new base takes it out of the merge queue, and whether it is behind, merges cleanly and has the checks it needs is worked out against the new base.

get.description:
What a pull request changes: the files it touches and their line-by-line diff against the commit it started from. Use it to review a pull request or to compare several made for the same work item. A large one lists every file (up to 300; truncated says when there were more) but has the lines of only the first, about 20,000 lines read: the files after that come with omitted true and no lines or counts. Ask again with paths (up to 50 at a time) to have those files' lines.

A file's `status` is `added`, `modified` or `deleted`. A binary file has no `hunks`. In a line, `old` is `null` when it was added and `new` is `null` when it was deleted.

post.description:
Ask more people or teams to review a pull request. `reviewers` are usernames; `team_reviewers` are teams, as `workspace/team` or the team's slug in the repository's workspace. They are added to whoever is asked already. Asking a team asks everyone in it, or with its review assignment on, the people it picks. Nobody is asked to review their own pull request, and a team must be one you can see. Whoever opened the pull request, or anyone with the Triage role or higher, while it is open. Returns the pull request, with `reviewers` and `team_reviewers` as they are now.

Adds to who is asked: `reviewers` by username (`g1t` asks a g1t agent), `team_reviewers` as `workspace/team`, or a team's slug in the repository's workspace. A team with review assignment on has the people it picks added to `reviewers`, and stays in `team_reviewers`. Each is told in their inbox. Nobody is asked to review their own pull request. `422` for someone who is not an account, or a team that does not exist or that you cannot see. Whoever opened it, or the Triage role or higher, while it is open. See [Pull requests](/guides/pull-requests/) and [Teams](/guides/teams/).

Its author may reopen their own, and whoever asked g1t for one may reopen that one; anyone else needs the Triage role or higher. Publishes pull.reopened with its head commit.

A merged pull request, or one that is not closed, answers `409`. A pull request closed as a draft comes back as a draft; any other comes back ready for review. A pull request from a branch of the repository whose branch was deleted answers `409` until the branch is pushed again. The same as `PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}` with `state` `open`.

post.description:
Land a pull request on its base, the branch it merges into (the default branch unless it names another). merge_method says how: merge (a merge commit joins its branch to the base, its commits included), squash (one new commit holds everything it changed), rebase (each of its commits is made again on top of the base, in order) or fast_forward (the base moves to its head, exactly the commit that was checked; only when its branch contains the base's head). Left out, the repository's default_merge_method. A method the repository does not allow (allow_merge_commit, allow_squash_merge, allow_rebase_merge, allow_fast_forward on update_repo_settings), or that a rule for the base does not (allowed_merge_methods, and required linear history, which refuses merge), is refused. commit_title and commit_message are a merge or squash commit's message: its first line and the rest; left out, the repository's merge_commit_message or squash_commit_message decides. With sha, the merge is refused (409) if the pull request's head is no longer that commit. delete_branch deletes its branch once it has merged (left out, the repository's delete_branch_on_merge); restore_pull_request_head_branch brings it back. Merging needs the Write role or higher, and only once it is marked ready and it meets every rule that holds for its base (see rules and required_checks on get_pull_request: approvals, checks, deployments, merge windows and the rest, from the repository's and its workspace's rulesets); the refusal names the first rule not met. With ignore_checks, someone who may merge can bypass required checks where the rule allows it; with bypass_rules, someone a ruleset lists as a bypass actor merges past its rules, and it is recorded. Merging into the default branch lands the work items in its closes in this repository: the work item it was made for (unless keep_item_open) and those its title and description name after a closing keyword (Fixes #12), where the repository does so (auto_close_items); each closes once it has landed in every target, and the other pull requests still in progress for its work item in this repository close as superseded. Merging into another branch closes nothing. Where the repository has a merge queue, a pull request into the default branch joins the queue instead of landing at once, to be tested and landed by merge_method (the merge queue rule's when absent) with the commit message given. If its base has moved since the pull request was opened, it is brought up to date first and lands when that is done; a repository that requires pull requests into its default branch to be up to date refuses instead: update_pull_request_branch, then merge again. Check status in the result to see whether it has landed, and merge_method and merge_commit for how.

A draft, or one whose checks have not passed, answers `409`. A pull request still `open` in the response has not landed yet: `landing` is true on it while it is brought up to date, and [get the merge queue](/reference/api/pull-requests/get-merge-queue/) shows it waiting in the [merge queue](/guides/merge-queue/). Merging lands the work items in `closes` in this repository and records it in their `resolutions` (into the default branch, where `auto_close_items` is on); each closes once it has landed in every target, and sets `superseded_by` on the pull requests it closes. A `merge_method` the repository or a rule for the base does not allow answers `422`, and a head that moved since `sha`, `409`. `merge_commit` is the commit the base is at afterwards: the merge or squash commit, the last rebased one, or the head for a fast-forward. See [Merging a pull request](/guides/pull-requests/#merging-a-pull-request).

`methods` are the repository's allowed methods, narrowed by the rules for the branch it merges into: required linear history leaves out `merge`. `fast_forward` lists `unavailable` until the branch contains its base's head. `merge` and `squash` carry the commit message a merge would use if you wrote none. put.description:
Bring a pull request's branch up to date with its base: update_method merge (the default) makes a merge commit on its branch that takes in the base's new commits; rebase makes each of its commits again on top of the base's head and moves its branch there, rewriting its history. Pushed as you, so you must be able to push to its branch: the Write role for a branch of the repository, its owner for a working copy, and push access to the fork for a branch of a fork. With expected_head_sha, refused (409) if its head is no longer that commit. Edits to the same file merge line by line; a rebase drops merge commits and commits the base already has, keeps authors, dates and messages, and moves its branch only if its head is still where it was. Returns outcome: updated (with commit, its head now, and previous), up_to_date, or needs_agent when both sides changed the same lines (with reason, detail and the paths): nothing was pushed, so merge or rebase in a clone and push.

`outcome` is `updated` (its branch moved from `previous` to `commit`), `up_to_date` (it already holds its base's head; `commit` only) or `needs_agent` (nothing was pushed: `reason` is `overlap`, `conflicting` or `unsupported`, with `detail` and the `paths` concerned). `update_method` `rebase` rewrites its branch, so pull it again before pushing more. A head that moved since `expected_head_sha` answers `409`. See [Keeping a pull request up to date](/guides/pull-requests/#keeping-it-up-to-date).

Needs the Write role, since it merges as you, and a repository that allows auto-merge (allow_auto_merge). A method the repository or a rule for its base does not allow is refused. A pull request that may merge already merges at once instead. Auto-merge is turned off when it merges or closes, when someone turns it off, and when someone other than whoever turned it on pushes to it. Publishes pull.auto_merge_enabled. Returns the pull request, with auto_merge saying how and who asked.

A repository with `allow_auto_merge` off answers `422`, as does a method it or a rule for the base does not allow. A pull request that may already merge merges at once: check `status`. `auto_merge` is cleared when it merges or closes, when it is turned off, and when someone other than `enabled_by` pushes to it. See [Auto-merge](/guides/pull-requests/#auto-merge).

put.description:
Change an artifact's content. For a doc: markdown with a target: append (add to the end), document (replace it all), section (with heading: that heading and everything under it) or blocks (from_block through to_block, block ids from its content). With the edit role the change is made, as a new version; with the comment role, or suggest_only, it is filed as a suggestion its editors accept or reject. note says why; marks_current says it brings the doc up to date with the code it cites. get.summary: Get who can open an artifact
get.description:
Who can open an artifact and how: its owner, each person, agent and team it is shared with (principal, role, and inherited_from when the access comes from a doc it is under), general_access (none, workspace or link) with general_role, whether it follows its space or parent (inherit), agent_mode, and whether you may change it (can_share).

Its owner always has full access and is not in `shared_with`. `inherited_from` on a row is the doc above it that gives that access; on the whole list, the space or doc it follows while `inherit` is true.

put.description:
Change who can open an artifact. Share it with a person (username), a team (team: its slug) or an agent (agent: its id), or a principal from its access list, at role view, comment, edit or manage (full access), with an optional notify message; role none takes theirs away. Set general_access to none (only people invited), workspace (everyone in the workspace) or link (anyone in the workspace with the link), with general_role view, comment or edit. inherit false stops it following its space or parent; true follows again. agent_mode suggest or edit says how agents change it (null follows its space). Takes full access (manage). Returns who can open it now.

One call can share with one person, team or agent, and change `general_access`, `inherit` and `agent_mode`, in that order. `role` set to `none` takes someone's access away. General access never gives full access. On an artifact that follows the doc it is under, change general access on that doc, or set `inherit` to false first.
